name: The Buddha
info: Siddhartha Gautama, called the Buddha, was a wandering religious teacher of the eastern Indo-Gangetic Plains in the 6th or 5th century BCE, remembered as the founder of Buddhism and its teacher of a Middle Way.

facts.born: Traditionally at Lumbini, now in Nepal, in the Shakya clan, the son of Śuddhodana; dates uncertain, 563–483 BCE in much early 20th-century scholarship
facts.died: Traditionally at Kushinagar, in modern Uttar Pradesh, aged about eighty, reaching parinirvana; the year is disputed
facts.role: Wandering religious teacher and founder of the saṅgha; held by Buddhists to be the Awakened One, described by historians as a śramaṇa teacher
facts.known: The awakening at Bodh Gaya; the first sermon at Sarnath; the Middle Way; the Four Noble Truths; the Noble Eightfold Path; dependent origination; the monastic order

t: According to Buddhist tradition, Siddhartha Gautama left a royal Shakya household, practised asceticism, and attained awakening at Bodh Gaya, after which he taught for the remaining forty or forty-five years of his life.
He taught a Middle Way between sensual indulgence and severe asceticism, and built a monastic order that later took in nuns as well as monks.
Scholars accept that he lived and taught during the reign of Bimbisara of Magadha, but they disagree about his dates and about how much of the early texts goes back to him.
dyk: The oldest surviving written record of the word Buddha is from the middle of the 3rd century BCE, in the Edicts of Ashoka, and Ashoka's Lumbini pillar inscription names the place as the Buddha's birthplace.
ev: Siddhartha Gautama is born, according to tradition at Lumbini, to a Shakya family
He leaves his home to live as a wandering ascetic, studying under Ārāḍa Kālāma and Udraka Rāmaputra
He attains awakening beneath a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya
He teaches the first sermon to five ascetics in the Deer Park at Sarnath, and the first saṅgha forms
King Bimbisara gives the community a bamboo grove, and Anāthapiṇḍika gives Jeta's grove
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī is ordained after Ānanda's request, founding the order of nuns
He dies at Kushinagar after a meal offered by the blacksmith Cunda, and is cremated
Ashoka's pillar at Lumbini records the site as the Buddha's birthplace

sections.early:
The Buddha is known by a clan name, Gautama (Pali: Gotama), a given name, Siddhārtha, and the title Buddha, 'the awakened one'. His dates are uncertain. A Sri Lankan long chronology gives 624–544 BCE, while most scholars who accept the long chronology but date Asoka's coronation around 268 BCE give 566–486 BCE. A short chronology from Indian sources gives 448–368 BCE, and many early 20th-century historians used 563–483 BCE.

According to Buddhist tradition, he was born in Lumbini, now in Nepal, and raised in Kapilavastu, among the Shakyas, a small community on the edge of the eastern Indian world. Later biographies call his father Śuddhodana a king and his mother Maya a princess from Devdaha. Many scholars think Śuddhodana was an aristocrat, perhaps an elected chief, of a republic and not a hereditary monarch.

The early texts say little about his youth. In them he recalls a very spoilt life in his parents' home. Several schools and later accounts give him a wife, Yasodhara, and a son, Rāhula. The Shakyas were annexed by the growing Kingdom of Kosala during his lifetime.
sections.rise:
The early texts give the reason for his leaving: he thought that life was subject to old age, disease and death and that there might be something better. His parents, they say, wept when he decided to go. The later biographies add the story of the four sights, an old man, a sick man, a corpse and an ascetic, which seems to be adapted from an account of an earlier Buddha, Vipassi.

As an ascetic he studied under two teachers, Ārāḍa Kālāma, who taught the sphere of nothingness, and Udraka Rāmaputra, who taught the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. He found neither enough. He then practised severe asceticism, with very little food, until his bones showed through his skin. According to the Mahāsaccaka-sutta and most of its parallels, he decided this had not helped him, and accepted food, a milk and rice pudding from a village girl named Sujata in one popular story. His five companions left him.

In Buddhist tradition he then sat beneath a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya and attained awakening. The later biographies add that Mara, the ruler of the desire realm, tried to prevent it by temptation and assault, and that the Buddha called the earth to witness.
sections.deeds:
The Buddhist texts say that he hesitated to teach, then agreed after the god Brahmā Sahampati urged him. He went to the Deer Park near Vārānasī and, according to several sources, taught the five ascetics the Middle Way, a path between sensual indulgence and self-mortification. The ascetic Kaundinya is said to have become the first arhat and the first monk, and the first saṅgha formed. When the community had grown to about sixty, he sent the monks out to teach for the welfare and benefit of the world.

For the remaining forty or forty-five years he is said to have travelled the Gangetic Plain, in what is now Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and southern Nepal, teaching nobles and servants, householders and ascetics. His order enjoyed the patronage of the kings of Kosala and Magadha. He is reported to have taught the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path, dependent origination, and that persons are a causal series of impermanent elements without a permanent self. He also taught lay people, in texts such as the Sigālovāda Sutta, about family, friendship and livelihood. The Pali suttas, as Bhikkhu Bodhi notes, do not teach only a world-transcending goal but also how laypersons may find worldly happiness.
sections.opponents:
The Buddha lived among many śramaṇa schools, among them the Ājīvikas, Jains and the sceptic Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, and the Pali canon often shows him in debate with their followers. On the way to Vārānasī, an Ājīvika named Upaka was not convinced when the Buddha said he had attained full awakening and took a different path.

He also criticised the Brahmins' claim of superior birth, held that the Vedas had no divine authority, and criticised animal sacrifice. Texts such as the Vasettha sutta say that one is a Brahmin by moral action and not by birth. According to Bronkhorst, however, the Brahmins did not occupy a dominant position in the region where he taught.

Trouble also came from inside his community. His cousin Devadatta is said to have tried to take over leadership of the order, left with several monks, and formed a rival sect, which the Pali texts say King Ajatashatru supported. They also say Devadatta plotted to kill the Buddha and failed. The Vinaya texts disagree about what Devadatta disputed.

Later scholars disagree about how much of the early texts goes back to the Buddha himself. Gombrich, Warder and Wynne think they contain material traceable to him, while Vetter, Schmithausen and Bronkhorst regard parts, such as the Four Noble Truths as a description of liberating insight, as later formulations.
sections.last:
The Mahaparinibbana Sutta (DN 16) and its parallels tell of his last year, a time of war, when Ajatashatru planned to attack the Vajjika League. The Buddha is said to have been ill, to have recovered at first, and to have refused to name a successor, telling Ānanda to live as an island unto himself, with the Dhamma as his refuge. Sariputta and Moggallana had died shortly before.

He ate his last meal as an offering from the blacksmith Cunda and fell violently ill. The texts do not blame the meal for his sickness, and they disagree about what it was: the Theravada tradition generally says some kind of pork, the Mahayana tradition a truffle or other mushroom, and modern scholars are divided. Mettanando and von Hinüber argue that he died of mesenteric infarction.

He went on to Kushinagar, where Ānanda prepared a resting place in a grove of sal trees. He ordained one last novice, Subhadda, repeated that the Dhamma and Vinaya should be the community's teacher, and asked if anyone had doubts. His reported last words are: 'All saṅkhāras decay. Strive for the goal with diligence.' Buddhists hold that he reached parinirvana, final release. The Mallians honoured his body, which was cremated after Mahākassapa arrived, and the relics were divided among several north Indian kingdoms and placed in stupas.
sections.legacy:
His teachings, passed down orally, were gathered into the Vinaya Piṭaka, the monastic code, and the Sūtra Piṭaka of discourses. Later generations added Abhidharma treatises, biographies, the Jataka tales of his past lives and the Mahāyāna sūtras. Buddhism developed into the Theravāda, Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna traditions and spread across Asia. It declined in India and largely disappeared there after the 8th century CE, while it grew more prominent in Southeast and East Asia.

The traditions see him differently. The earliest texts do not describe him as omniscient or as an eternal transcendent being. Mahāyāna texts present Śākyamuni as a cosmic being whose birth and death were skilful teaching devices. Theravada countries celebrate the day of his birth, awakening and death as Vesak, and in Nepal, Bangladesh and India it is Buddha Purnima.

Other religions have placed him in their own histories. He was incorporated into Vaishnavism as the 9th avatar of Vishnu. The Christian saint Josaphat is based on him. Muslim writers called him Budd, and Rashid al-Din saw him as a monotheistic prophet. The Baháʼí Faith regards him as one of the Manifestations of God, and Manichaeism listed him among the prophets before Mani.

His early images were aniconic: an empty throne, footprints, a Dharma wheel or a Bodhi tree. Images in human form became popular after the first century CE.

summary: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught in the Gangetic Plain in the 6th or 5th century BCE and built a monastic order. Scholars accept that he lived and taught under King Bimbisara, but dispute his dates and how much of the early texts reflects his own teaching.
references: Patrick Olivelle, Life of the Buddha by Ashva-ghosha (New York University Press, 2008)
André Bareau, Recherches sur la biographie du Buddha dans les Sutrapitaka et les Vinayapitaka anciens (Ecole Francaise d'Extreme-Orient, 1963)
Carol Anderson, Pain and Its Ending: The Four Noble Truths in the Theravada Buddhist Canon (Routledge, 1999)
notes: Dates: the article gives several chronologies (624-544, 566-486, 563-483, 448-368, c. 410 death). I used the early 20th-century 563-483 BCE with circa on both years.
The ev line "In early adulthood" gives no age because the article does not.
'The Buddha called the earth to witness' is the later biographies' account, attributed as such.
Left out: the 32 marks, Mahayana trikaya detail beyond one sentence, Islamic identifications beyond Rashid al-Din, previous lives beyond the Jataka mention.
